cardBlurb: ABAQUS UMAT for aluminum stretch forming.
cat: Research: BITS Pilani, with IIT Madras
title: Failure Prediction in Sheet Metal Forming

body.caption: Von Mises stress contour at 20mm dome height

body: I expected the highest strain and thinning to show up at the center of the dome, where the sheet gets stretched the most. Instead the thickness data showed more reduction a bit further out from the center, meaning the material was actually more likely to fail there than at the apex.

I did this project to look at why aluminum sheets are harder to form than steel at room temperature, even though they are lighter and more corrosion resistant, which matters for automotive body panels. I built a finite element model in ABAQUS of a standard stretch forming setup, a 1mm thick AA5754-H22 aluminum sheet formed with a 50mm punch, along with the blank holder and die.

body.caption: Stretch forming assembly: punch, blank holder, and die

body: I only modeled a 90 degree quarter of the part to keep the run time reasonable. Before running the forming simulation I did a mesh independency check across four mesh sizes and also ran a separate tensile test simulation to get the material stress strain behavior using Swifts law.

At a dome height of 20mm, the von Mises stress plot showed a clear ring of high stress at the sheet to die interface rather than at the center. The strain also increased moving away from the center, with a small spike around 30mm caused by the sheet bending against the die. Comparing my simulated stress strain curve to the actual experimental data for this material, the two matched well early on but started to diverge at higher strain.

When I tried extending the simulation to predict actual failure, I ran into a time increment error, likely from the boundary conditions or a units issue, and I also noticed the sheet slipping between the holder and die during stretching. Both point to the same next step, adding a drawbead and a proper clamping step before the punch starts moving.
